c-surg-08-q043.hinge: Primary hyperthyroidism (elevated T4, suppressed TSH) in the presence of a single thyroid nodule indicates an autonomous hyperfunctioning thyroid adenoma (toxic adenoma).
c-surg-08-q043.trap: Symptoms of hyperthyroidism tempt Graves disease, but a solitary thyroid nodule without diffuse goiter or orbitopathy points to toxic adenoma.

A.fit: Not here: causes goiter and hypothyroidism, not overt thyrotoxicosis
A.tempting: congenital thyroid enzyme defect

B.clue: TSH-receptor autoantibody stimulation causing diffuse goiter
B.fit: Not here: single solitary nodule, lacks diffuse enlargement or ophthalmopathy

C.fit: Not here: examination clearly shows a single isolated nodule

D.clue: Dense IgG4-related fibrous replacement of thyroid
D.fit: Not here: presents as fixed woody goiter with hypothyroidism

E.fit: Not here: thyroid cancers are typically cold and euthyroid
E.tempting: single palpable nodule in a young male

F.fit: Not here: thyroid cysts do not hypersecrete thyroid hormone

G.clue: Transient release of preformed hormone with neck pain
G.fit: Not here: 6-month indolent duration, painless solitary nodule

H.clue: Solitary autonomous nodule hypersecreting thyroid hormone
H.fit: Here: solitary nodule, suppressed TSH, high T4, thyrotoxic symptoms

I.clue: Isolated elevation of T3 with normal thyroxine

nodes.text: Hyperthyroid symptoms (palpitations, weight loss, tremor) + single palpable thyroid nodule
Confirm primary hyperthyroidism: suppressed serum TSH + elevated free T4 or T3
Perform radioactive iodine uptake and scan: focal hot nodule with suppressed background uptake
Initiate beta-blocker therapy (e.g. propranolol) for acute adrenergic symptom control
**Definitive therapy in surgical candidate:** unilateral thyroid lobectomy after achieving euthyroid state
**Definitive therapy in nonsurgical candidate:** radioactive iodine ablation
Fine-needle aspiration is not indicated for autonomously functioning hot nodules due to near-zero malignancy risk

single thyroid nodule

c-surg-08-q044.boardCall: Post-thyroidectomy circumoral paresthesia + positive Chvostek sign -> Intravenous calcium gluconate
c-surg-08-q044.hinge: Acute symptomatic hypocalcemia (circumoral numbness, fingertip paresthesias, positive Chvostek sign) after total thyroidectomy requires immediate intravenous calcium gluconate to prevent tetany or seizures.
c-surg-08-q044.trap: Mild symptoms tempt oral calcium carbonate or vitamin D, but active neuromotor excitability mandates immediate IV calcium.

A.clue: Immediate intravenous membrane-stabilizing calcium repletion
A.fit: Here: 24 h post-thyroidectomy, perioral paresthesias, positive Chvostek sign

B.clue: Intravenous repletion for symptomatic hypomagnesemia
B.fit: Not here: primary etiology is acute postsurgical hypoparathyroidism
B.tempting: hypomagnesemia can contribute to refractory hypocalcemia

C.clue: Oral calcium repletion for mild maintenance
C.fit: Not here: oral absorption too slow for acute symptomatic neuroirritability
C.tempting: first-line for chronic or asymptomatic mild hypocalcemia

D.clue: Oral mineral repletion for mild magnesium deficiency
D.fit: Not here: fails to treat acute life-threatening post-surgical hypocalcemia
D.tempting: adjunctive mineral in parathyroid disorders

E.clue: Vitamin D facilitating intestinal calcium absorption
E.fit: Not here: slow onset; given as adjunctive maintenance after IV calcium
E.tempting: essential for long-term hypoparathyroidism management

nodes.text: Circumoral paresthesias + carpopedal spasm + Chvostek sign after thyroidectomy
IV calcium gluconate slowly under continuous cardiac monitoring
Check serum magnesium, ionized calcium, PTH
**Low magnesium:** replace magnesium to restore parathyroid responsiveness
**Symptoms recur after IV bolus:** continuous IV calcium gluconate infusion
Oral calcium carbonate + calcitriol for maintenance
Serial ionized calcium until stable

circumoral paresthesia and tingling of the fingertips
hyperreflexia when the facial nerve is tapped

c-surg-08-q045.boardCall: Post-thoracotomy oliguria with normal BUN and creatinine -> ADH (vasopressin)
c-surg-08-q045.hinge: Major surgical stress, thoracic trauma, severe pain, and opioids stimulate nonosmotic release of ADH (vasopressin), producing transient oliguria with normal renal function.
c-surg-08-q045.trap: Oliguria tempts sympathetic hormones, but direct renal water reabsorption with concentrated urine is mediated by ADH.

A.clue: Posterior pituitary hormone promoting collecting duct water reabsorption
A.fit: Here: post-thoracotomy oliguria, normal creatinine 0.9, normal BUN 12

B.clue: Adrenocortical glucocorticoid promoting gluconeogenesis and anti-inflammatory response
B.fit: Not here: elevated in surgical stress, but does not drive acute oliguria
B.tempting: classic corticosteroid released during major surgical trauma

C.clue: Adrenal medullary catecholamine increasing heart rate
C.fit: Not here: primary cardiovascular mediator; does not directly cause renal water retention
C.tempting: elevated during surgical stress and pain

D.clue: Pancreatic alpha cell hormone promoting glycogenolysis
D.fit: Not here: metabolic regulator of glucose, not renal water excretion
D.tempting: stress-induced metabolic hormone

E.clue: Sympathetic neurotransmitter inducing systemic arteriolar vasoconstriction
E.fit: Not here: causes systemic vasoconstriction, but direct water retention is ADH-driven
E.tempting: mediated by sympathetic activation after trauma

nodes.text: Postoperative oliguria with normal BUN and creatinine after thoracic trauma or surgery
Pain, surgical stress, and opioids trigger nonosmotic ADH (vasopressin) release
ADH acts on V2 receptors, inserting aquaporin-2 to reabsorb water
**Hyponatremia with concentrated urine, euvolemic:** avoid hypotonic fluids, restrict free water
**Hypotension or rising creatinine:** evaluate hypovolemia or ATN; isotonic fluid challenge
Effective multimodal analgesia; avoid excessive fluid boluses

triggers.text: Two days after undergoing thoracotomy for a stab wound
oliguria despite adequate fluid replacement
serum urea nitrogen concentration is 12 mg/dL, and serum creatinine concentration is 0.9 mg/dL
received 4 units of packed red blood cells

c-surg-08-q046.boardCall: Severe acute hyponatremia with seizures after neurosurgery -> 3% Sodium chloride
c-surg-08-q046.hinge: Severe symptomatic hyponatremia (Na 118 mEq/L with tonic-clonic seizures) from SIADH requires emergent intravenous hypertonic (3%) sodium chloride to halt cerebral edema.
c-surg-08-q046.trap: Seizures and VP shunt revision tempt barbiturate coma or antiseizure medication alone, but acute hyponatremic encephalopathy requires hypertonic saline.

A.clue: Synthetic ADH analogue promoting renal water reabsorption
A.fit: Not here: contraindicated; worsens water retention and exacerbates hyponatremia
A.tempting: used for diabetes insipidus

B.clue: Hypotonic fluid source providing carbohydrate calories
B.fit: Not here: administration of free water worsens hypoosmolar hyponatremia
B.tempting: common initial IV fluid

C.clue: Pure opioid receptor antagonist reversing narcotic effects
C.fit: Not here: does not treat severe hyponatremic encephalopathy or seizures
C.tempting: patient is receiving continuous morphine infusion

D.clue: Barbiturate used for refractory status epilepticus
D.fit: Not here: fails to address underlying fatal hyponatremic cerebral edema
D.tempting: suppresses tonic-clonic seizure activity

E.clue: Hypertonic saline rapidly expanding serum osmolality
E.fit: Here: Na 118 mEq/L, seizures, SIADH following neurosurgery

nodes.text: Acute severe hyponatremia (serum Na < 120 mEq/L) presenting with seizures, coma, or encephalopathy
Immediately administer 3% hypertonic saline bolus to raise serum sodium by 4-6 mEq/L
Re-evaluate neurologic status and serum sodium every 1-2 hours
Limit total correction rate to < 8-10 mEq/L in 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome
**Fluid-overloaded state (heart failure, cirrhosis):** add intravenous loop diuretics
**Euvolemic SIADH after acute symptoms resolve:** implement fluid restriction

triggers.text: generalized tonic-clonic seizures and a decreased urine output 24 hours after undergoing revision
Serum Na 118 mEq/L
central venous pressure of 9 cm H₂O
continuous morphine infusion for pain

c-surg-08-q047.boardCall: Potassium 6.6 mEq/L + peaked T waves on ECG -> Intravenous calcium chloride therapy
c-surg-08-q047.hinge: Severe hyperkalemia (K 6.6 mEq/L) with electrocardiographic changes (peaked T waves) is an immediate cardiac emergency requiring intravenous calcium for myocardial membrane stabilization.
c-surg-08-q047.trap: Acute renal failure tempts hemodialysis, and high lab value tempts repeating potassium, but membrane stabilization with IV calcium is the mandatory first step.

A.clue: Confirmatory repeat phlebotomy to exclude pseudohyperkalemia
A.fit: Not here: peaked T waves confirm true hyperkalemic cardiotoxicity
A.tempting: rules out in vitro hemolysis

B.clue: Dietary restriction limiting potassium intake
B.fit: Not here: far too slow for acute hyperkalemic cardiotoxicity
B.tempting: chronic hyperkalemia maintenance strategy

C.clue: Cation-exchange resin binding gastrointestinal potassium
C.fit: Not here: slow onset, risk of colonic necrosis postoperatively
C.tempting: eliminates potassium from the body

D.clue: Direct cardiac membrane stabilization antagonizing potassium cardiotoxicity
D.fit: Here: K 6.6 mEq/L with peaked T waves on ECG

E.clue: Extracorporeal filtration for definitive potassium clearance
E.fit: Not here: stabilize cardiac membrane with IV calcium first before dialysis
E.tempting: definitive clearance in acute renal failure

nodes.text: K 6.6 mEq/L with peaked T waves: hyperkalemic emergency
IV calcium chloride or gluconate to stabilize myocardium
**Suspected hemolyzed sample without ECG changes:** repeat potassium measurement
Shift potassium: IV insulin + dextrose, nebulized albuterol
**Concurrent metabolic acidosis:** IV sodium bicarbonate
Remove potassium: loop diuretic or oral binder
**End-stage renal disease or oliguria:** urgent hemodialysis

creatinine concentration of 3 mg/dL
peaked T waves across the precordium
transurethral resection of the prostate

c-surg-08-q048.boardCall: Severe hypotension + tachycardia + dropping hematocrit + low CVP 8 hours after laparoscopy -> Postoperative bleeding
c-surg-08-q048.hinge: Acute hypotension (60/40 mm Hg), tachycardia (150/min), acute drop in hematocrit from 42% to 28%, and low central venous pressure (2 mm Hg) within 8 hours of laparoscopy confirm postoperative intra-abdominal hemorrhage.
c-surg-08-q048.trap: Tachycardia, hypoxemia, and postoperative state tempt pulmonary embolism or MI, but low CVP and acute 14-point drop in hematocrit confirm hemorrhagic shock.

A.clue: Acute adrenocortical insufficiency with refractory hypotension
A.fit: Not here: acute drop in hematocrit demonstrates major blood loss
A.tempting: refractory postoperative circulatory collapse

B.clue: Acute myocardial necrosis causing cardiogenic shock
B.fit: Not here: normal CK-MB fraction, low CVP (2 mm Hg), acute anemia
B.tempting: severe hypotension and tachycardia post-surgery

C.clue: Hemorrhagic shock from surgical vessel injury
C.fit: Here: hematocrit drop from 42% to 28%, CVP 2 mm Hg, shock

D.clue: Thromboembolic occlusion of pulmonary arterial bed
D.fit: Not here: PE causes elevated CVP and right ventricular strain; CVP is 2
D.tempting: sudden tachycardia and PO2 70 mm Hg

E.clue: Vasodilatory shock from overwhelming systemic infection
E.fit: Not here: afebrile at 8 hours, sudden 14-point hematocrit drop
E.tempting: postoperative hypotension with severe tachycardia

**High CVP, hypoxemia, tachycardia:** suspect pulmonary embolism; CT angiography
**Fever, leukocytosis, warm extremities:** septic shock; cultures + antibiotics
**Chronic steroid use, fluid-refractory hypotension:** adrenal crisis; IV hydrocortisone
Massive transfusion protocol with balanced blood products
Emergent re-exploration to ligate bleeding source (cystic artery, liver bed)
Correct hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy

pulse of 150/min and blood pressure of 60/40 mm Hg
Hematocrit is 28% (42% preoperatively)
Central venous pressure is 2 mm Hg.

c-surg-08-q049.boardCall: Incapacitated trauma patient in hemorrhagic shock + unverified friend report -> Transfusion of packed red blood cells
c-surg-08-q049.hinge: In an incapacitated patient with life-threatening hemorrhagic shock and no formal signed advance directive or durable power of attorney, emergency doctrine mandates life-saving blood transfusion regardless of a bystander's uncertain belief.
c-surg-08-q049.trap: Friend's statement tempts withholding blood or urgent ethics consultation, but life-saving blood products must not be delayed based on uncertain hearsay.

A.fit: Not here: emergency resuscitation cannot be delayed for committee review
A.tempting: ethical conflict regarding religious objection to transfusion

B.clue: Crystalloid or colloid infusion without blood products
B.fit: Not here: hematocrit 15% in hemorrhagic shock requires oxygen-carrying capacity
B.tempting: avoids blood products in potential Jehovah's Witness

C.clue: Emergency life-saving administration of allogeneic erythrocytes
C.fit: Here: incapacitated, shock (BP 75/40, Hct 15%), unverified friend report

Evaluate for legally binding refusal: signed advance directive card or designated durable power of attorney
**Valid signed refusal card present:** respect patient autonomy; resuscitate with non-blood volume expanders
**No official documentation in incapacitated patient:** apply emergency doctrine and administer life-saving blood transfusion
Proceed directly to emergent operative intervention (exploratory laparotomy) for surgical hemorrhage control
Document clinical emergency rationale thoroughly in medical record

c-surg-08-q050.trap: Need for tracheostomy tempts emergency doctrine or ethics committee consent, but this is a semi-elective decision and an identified surrogate exists who must be contacted.

A.fit: Not here: prolonged intubation causes vocal cord damage and subglottic stenosis

B.fit: Here: incapacitated patient, nonemergent tracheostomy, reachable next of kin

C.fit: Not here: ethics committees do not provide legal consent when surrogate exists

D.tempting: attempts to ascertain direct patient wishes

abdominal-trauma.name: Abdominal trauma
abdominal-trauma.scope: Blunt abdominal trauma (splenic/hepatic laceration, FAST exam, CT scan), penetrating abdominal trauma (stab, gunshot, peritonitis, exploratory laparotomy indications)
abdominal-trauma.core: Abdominal injury after collision, fall, stabbing, or gunshot: hemodynamic status and peritoneal signs determine imaging versus immediate operation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: High-speed deceleration, seat-belt compression, lower rib fractures; anticoagulation increases bleeding risk
Stab wounds may spare viscera; bullets frequently injure multiple structures

rows.label: Clues
items: LUQ pain or referred left shoulder pain → splenic injury; RUQ tenderness → hepatic injury
Distention, ecchymoses, abdominal wall marks; initially benign examination does not exclude bowel injury
★ **Rigidity, rebound, persistent hypotension**, or evisceration → urgent operative assessment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Solid-organ disruption → intraperitoneal hemorrhage; mesenteric injury → ischemia or delayed perforation
Retroperitoneal injury may produce little intraperitoneal free fluid

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **FAST** at bedside during resuscitation; detects free fluid, not organ-specific injury
★ Stable → **CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast**; evaluate solid organs, bowel, retroperitoneum
Negative FAST with ongoing shock → search thorax/pelvis, repeat assessment; do not assume safety
Stable anterior stab → local wound exploration or serial examination/CT; trajectory guides evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: Airway, large-bore IV access, warmed blood products; massive transfusion for hemorrhagic shock
★ Unstable + positive FAST, peritonitis, or ongoing transfusion need → **exploratory laparotomy**; no CT delay
Stable splenic/hepatic injury → monitored nonoperative care; blush, transient response → angioembolization (older questions: laparotomy)
Enteric contents, uncontrolled bleeding → operation; transperitoneal gunshot → **laparotomy** even if stable; selected stabs observed
Suspected bowel perforation → ceftriaxone + metronidazole, trauma surgery; free subdiaphragmatic air → **laparotomy**, no CT

rows.label: Complications
items: Delayed splenic rupture, abscess, bile leak, abdominal compartment syndrome
Missed hollow-viscus injury → sepsis; splenectomy → overwhelming encapsulated bacterial infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Restraints, airbags, injury-prevention counseling
★ After splenectomy → **pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib vaccines**; fever requires urgent antibiotics

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pelvic hemorrhage: unstable pelvis, negative abdominal FAST
Tension pneumothorax: unilateral absent breath sounds, obstructive shock

abdominal-trauma.evidence: Not checked online; established trauma assessment and management principles.

acute-coronary-syndromes.name: Acute coronary syndromes
acute-coronary-syndromes.scope: Unstable angina, NSTEMI, STEMI, cardiac biomarkers, risk stratification (HEART/TIMI), antiplatelet and anticoagulation, reperfusion
acute-coronary-syndromes.core: Acute myocardial ischemia from coronary plaque disruption: distinguish occlusive infarction needing immediate reperfusion from non-ST-elevation syndromes needing risk-guided invasive management.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, CKD, age, premature family CAD
Cocaine/stimulants, anemia, tachyarrhythmia may provoke ischemia; distinguish supply-demand injury from plaque rupture

rows.label: Clues
items: Pressure with arm/jaw radiation, diaphoresis, nausea; older adults/diabetes may have dyspnea or epigastric pain alone
Inferior MI with hypotension, clear lungs, raised JVP → suspect RV infarction
★ New murmur, pulmonary edema, shock after MI → **mechanical complication**, urgent echo
Unexplained crash/syncope + ischemic ECG → primary MI; troponin over trauma imaging

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Platelet activation and thrombin-mediated clot reduce coronary perfusion; necrosis releases troponin
Type 2 MI: oxygen mismatch without acute atherothrombosis; treat precipitating cause

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ECG within 10 minutes**, repeat if nondiagnostic; serial high-sensitivity troponin using validated pathway
Posterior suspicion → V7–V9; inferior MI → right-sided leads; new LBBB alone insufficient for STEMI
★ **Do not wait for troponin before STEMI reperfusion**; bedside echo if diagnosis/complications uncertain
HEART ≤3 + negative serial troponins → low risk; TIMI/GRACE stratifies NSTE-ACS
STE: **V1–V6 → LAD**; **II, III, aVF + bradycardia → RCA**; I, aVL → circumflex

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Chewed aspirin**, P2Y12 inhibitor, anticoagulant such as heparin, high-intensity atorvastatin; oxygen only if hypoxemic
Nitroglycerin (**venodilation** → ↓preload) for pain unless hypotension, RV infarction, recent PDE5 inhibitor; avoid NSAIDs
★ STEMI → **primary PCI** within 90 minutes at PCI center, ≤120 minutes including transfer
IF PCI delay >120 minutes, symptoms <12 hours, no contraindication → fibrinolysis promptly, then transfer

rows.label: Complications
items: VT/VF, AV block, HF, cardiogenic shock; free-wall rupture
Later aneurysm/thrombus, embolism, Dressler syndrome; antithrombotics → bleeding
Post-MI murmur: **papillary rupture** → apical, no O₂ step-up; **septal rupture** → left sternal, RA→RV step-up

rows.label: Prevention
items: DAPT usually 12 months after ACS unless bleeding risk changes plan; cardiac rehabilitation, smoking cessation
ACE inhibitor/ARB for LV dysfunction; beta-blocker when stable, avoid in shock or acute decompensation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Aortic dissection: abrupt tearing pain/pulse deficit; anticoagulation or lysis dangerous
Pericarditis: positional pleuritic pain, diffuse changes
PE: hypoxemia, thrombotic risk, RV strain

table.title: Syndrome branches
rows: Urgent catheterization if unstable; otherwise risk-guided angiography
Regional ST elevation or occlusion equivalent
Prior intracranial hemorrhage, active bleeding, suspected dissection
Stress or perfusion testing within 72 hours

acute-kidney-injury.name: Acute kidney injury
acute-kidney-injury.core: Abrupt loss of renal filtration: separate impaired perfusion, parenchymal injury, and urinary obstruction before treating the cause.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Volume depletion, sepsis, cirrhosis, low-output heart failure (prerenal despite overload); baseline CKD increases vulnerability
NSAIDs constrict afferent arterioles; ACE inhibitors/ARBs reduce efferent tone during hypoperfusion
Aminoglycosides, pigment (dipstick blood, few RBCs), prolonged ischemia → tubular damage; antibiotics/PPIs → tubulointerstitial inflammation

rows.label: Clues
items: Oliguria, edema, uremic nausea; urine output may remain normal
AIN: fever, rash, eosinophilia sometimes present; classic triad often absent
★ Pulmonary edema, severe hyperkalemia, encephalopathy, pericarditis → **urgent renal support**
Anuria despite patent catheter after pelvic surgery + hydronephrosis → ureteral injury/ligation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced glomerular pressure, tubular epithelial injury, or backpressure → declining GFR

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ AKI: creatinine ↑≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 h, ≥1.5-fold within 7 days, or oliguria
Oliguria criterion: urine <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥6 h; trend creatinine, electrolytes, fluid balance
★ **Urinalysis + microscopy**, medication review; bladder scan → renal ultrasound if obstruction possible
FeNa unreliable with diuretics, CKD, early obstruction; urine eosinophils neither sensitive nor specific
Unexplained persistent injury or suspected glomerulonephritis → nephrology, possible kidney biopsy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe hyperkalemia → **IV calcium**, insulin/dextrose; refractory electrolyte disturbance → dialysis
Hypovolemia (postoperative oliguria, high urine specific gravity) → saline bolus; congestion → loop diuretic; no reflex fluids in overload
Stop nephrotoxins, all NSAIDs including celecoxib (intra-articular steroid for joint pain); persistent AIN → glucocorticoids; renal-dose drugs
★ Obstruction → **catheter or ureteral decompression**; monitor postobstructive diuresis
Dialysis: refractory acidosis, hyperkalemia, intoxication, overload, symptomatic uremia; no isolated creatinine threshold

rows.label: Complications
items: Arrhythmias, acidosis, volume overload; subsequent CKD
Recovery diuresis → dehydration and electrolyte losses

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintain perfusion during illness; review nephrotoxic combinations and monitor renal function
Contrast in high-risk CKD → **periprocedural IV isotonic saline**; diuretics, mannitol, metformin stop don't protect
ACR now limits contrast prophylaxis mainly to eGFR <30; older exam questions may expect wider hydration

rows.label: Mimics
items: CKD: longstanding abnormalities, small echogenic kidneys, chronic anemia
Trimethoprim effect: creatinine rise without true GFR decline

acute-kidney-injury.evidence: Not checked online; established KDIGO diagnostic criteria and renal teaching.

acute-respiratory-failure.name: Acute respiratory failure
acute-respiratory-failure.scope: Hypoxemic respiratory failure (type 1), hypercapnic respiratory failure (type 2), noninvasive positive pressure ventilation (BiPAP/CPAP), indications for invasive mechanical ventilation
acute-respiratory-failure.core: Acute inability to maintain oxygenation or ventilation demands simultaneous cause treatment and escalating respiratory support, guided by work of breathing and airway safety.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pneumonia, pulmonary edema, ARDS, PE → oxygenation failure
COPD, neuromuscular weakness, obesity hypoventilation, sedatives → ventilation failure; overlap common

rows.label: Clues
items: Tachypnea, accessory-muscle use, hypoxemia, diaphoresis; hypercapnia may cause headache, somnolence, asterixis
★ **Exhaustion, declining consciousness, silent chest, paradoxical breathing** → impending respiratory arrest
Normal saturation on supplemental oxygen does not exclude dangerous CO₂ retention

rows.label: Pathophys
items: V/Q mismatch, shunt, or diffusion impairment lowers PaO₂; shunt may resist oxygen alone
Inadequate alveolar ventilation raises PaCO₂; abrupt rise causes respiratory acidosis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pulse oximetry + ABG** when severe distress, hypercapnia concern, or escalating support
Chest radiograph, ECG, bedside lung/cardiac ultrasound; infection/PE testing follows clinical context
Trend pH, gases, respiratory rate, mentation and effort; do not wait for an extreme number
Chronic compensated hypercapnia has elevated bicarbonate; pH decline identifies acute deterioration

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Oxygen immediately**, treat cause; target SpO₂ 88–92% with CO₂-retention risk, usually 92–96% otherwise
Hypoxemic failure needing more than conventional oxygen → high-flow nasal cannula, close reassessment
★ Awake cooperative COPD + respiratory acidosis → **BiPAP**; cardiogenic edema → CPAP/BiPAP plus diuresis/nitrates
★ **Intubate** for airway failure, refractory hypoxemia, shock, arrest, exhaustion, or worsening despite noninvasive support
Avoid NIV with vomiting, unprotected airway, copious secretions, major facial trauma; reassess within 1–2 h

rows.label: Complications
items: Hypoxic brain injury, arrhythmia, multiorgan failure; delayed intubation worsens outcome
Positive pressure → hypotension/barotrauma; invasive ventilation → pneumonia and ventilator-induced lung injury
Ventilated ARDS: low tidal volume using predicted body weight, limited plateau pressure; prone if severe

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, respiratory vaccination, disease control, cautious sedatives, aspiration precautions
High-risk extubation patients may benefit from planned NIV rather than rescue after deterioration
Awake, stable, low ventilator support → **spontaneous breathing trial** to wean, before tracheostomy

rows.label: Mimics
items: Metabolic acidosis: compensatory tachypnea with low CO₂
Panic hyperventilation: respiratory alkalosis without sustained gas-exchange failure

table.title: Gas-exchange classification; room air when feasible

advance-directives-and-surrogates.name: Advance directives and surrogate decisions
advance-directives-and-surrogates.scope: Living will, DNR/DNI orders, health care proxy, substituted judgment, best interests, advance care planning
advance-directives-and-surrogates.core: Follow the capable patient's current wishes; when capacity is absent, use valid directives and authorized surrogate judgment.

rows.label: Principle
items: Autonomy persists after incapacity through documented preferences and legally authorized decision-makers
Substituted judgment: patient's known values; best interests: benefits/burdens when preferences unknown

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Confirm capacity, directive validity, clinical applicability, and designated **health care proxy**
★ Apply the patient's instructions over conflicting surrogate preferences
Discuss goals, code status, surrogate early; terminal sole caregiver → plan **child guardianship**

rows.label: Don't
items: ★ **DNR limits CPR**; do not automatically withhold antibiotics, analgesia, nutrition, or other treatment
Dementia diagnosis, mild test errors, or disagreement ≠ incapacity; capacity is decision-specific
★ **Surrogate cannot compel contraindicated treatment** → withhold it; ethics consult unnecessary

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Capable patient may revise prior instructions; current informed choices control
No directive/proxy → adult next of kin; none eligible (minor relative) → **court guardian**
Clear directive/reported wishes/proxy–team agreement → no consult; unresolved conflict → ethics, court

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **DNI and DNR differ**; clarify acceptable ventilation and perioperative plans
Proxy needs no terminal illness; dementia tube-feeding request → review lack of benefit, harms
Surrogate conveys patient's known wishes, not own beliefs; missing paperwork doesn't block them

Portable treatment orders for serious illness

anorectal-disorders.name: Anorectal disorders
anorectal-disorders.scope: Anal fissure, internal and external hemorrhoids, anorectal abscess, fistula-in-ano, pruritus ani, topical vasodilators, fiber, sitz baths
anorectal-disorders.core: Anal pain, bleeding, swelling, or drainage requires inspection and focused examination; pain pattern distinguishes fissure, thrombosis, and infection.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Constipation, straining, pregnancy, prolonged sitting; Crohn disease, diabetes, immunosuppression increase infection risk
Irritant soaps, moisture, fecal seepage contribute to pruritus ani

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Pain out of proportion, fever, spreading erythema, crepitus** → evaluate necrotizing perineal infection urgently
Posterior midline fissure common; lateral/multiple fissures suggest Crohn disease, infection, or malignancy
Internal hemorrhoids lie above dentate line; prolapse may require manual reduction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fissure causes internal sphincter spasm and local ischemia; hemorrhoids represent enlarged vascular cushions
Cryptoglandular infection creates abscess; persistent epithelialized tract can become a fistula

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Inspection first**, gentle DRE/anoscopy when tolerable; do not force painful fissure examination
Deep pain without visible lesion → CT/MRI for occult abscess; recurrent fistula → pelvic MRI
Rectal bleeding with anemia, weight loss, bowel change, or screening indication → colon evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Fiber, fluids, stool softening, **sitz baths**; fissure → topical anesthetic, nitroglycerin or diltiazem
Refractory chronic fissure → botulinum toxin or lateral internal sphincterotomy after continence-risk assessment
Internal hemorrhoids persisting despite conservative measures → rubber-band ligation; advanced prolapse → surgery
★ Abscess → **incision and drainage**; antibiotics added for cellulitis, systemic illness, or immunosuppression
Fistula → colorectal surgery; painful thrombosed external hemorrhoid within 72 hours → consider excision

rows.label: Complications
items: Abscess recurrence, fistula, sepsis; sphincter injury → fecal incontinence
Chronic bleeding → iron deficiency; pruritus → excoriations and secondary infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid straining and prolonged toilet sitting; gentle cleansing, dry skin, barrier ointment for seepage

rows.label: Mimics
items: Anal cancer: persistent irregular ulcer/mass or large wart-like lesion, biopsy required
Proctitis: urgency, tenesmus, mucous discharge
Pinworm: nocturnal itch, especially children; tape test

table.title: Local patterns
rows: Tearing defecation pain; bright blood on paper
Recurrent purulent drainage from external opening

benign-breast-conditions.name: Benign breast conditions
benign-breast-conditions.scope: Fibroadenoma, fibrocystic changes, intraductal papilloma, breast cyst, fat necrosis, galactocele, breast abscess
benign-breast-conditions.core: Breast symptoms require age-directed imaging and clinical–radiologic concordance; a benign-appearing examination alone cannot exclude malignancy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Reproductive hormonal cycling; milk stasis; breast trauma or prior surgery
Smoking predisposes to recurrent subareolar abscess
**Cracked, excoriated nipples** → main portal of entry for lactational mastitis

rows.label: Clues
items: Galactocele: cystic lactational/postlactational mass, no inflammation, varies with feeds; fat–fluid level on imaging
Mastitis: focal tender erythema, fever, no fluctuance; abscess adds **fluctuance**; often Staphylococcus aureus
★ Spontaneous unilateral **bloody single-duct discharge** → usually **papilloma**; exclude malignancy, persistent → surgical evaluation
Nonbloody discharge only on expression, normal exam → **physiologic**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hormone-responsive stromal/glandular tissue produces cyclic changes; duct obstruction causes retained secretions
Adipose injury causes inflammatory necrosis and calcification that can resemble cancer

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Palpable mass **<30 years → ultrasound**; ≥30 → diagnostic mammography with targeted ultrasound
Suspicious solid lesion or imaging–exam discordance → **core needle biopsy**
Simple cyst: anechoic, thin-walled, posterior enhancement; no solid component
Nonlactational abscess or persistent inflammation after antibiotics → exclude underlying carcinoma
Cyclic bilateral nodularity, no dominant mass → **reexamine after menses**, before imaging

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Painful simple cyst → aspiration; nonbloody fluid + full collapse → benign; bloody fluid/residual mass → **biopsy**
Fibroadenoma → observe when concordant; excise if rapidly enlarging, large or symptomatic
Breast pain, no mass, young, normal exam → **reassurance**; fibrocystic pain → supportive bra, topical/oral NSAID
★ Mastitis → **dicloxacillin/cephalexin**, keep breastfeeding/pumping; abscess → add needle/incision drainage; MRSA → clindamycin
Tender lactating lump, no erythema/fever → **warm compresses**, keep nursing; persistent galactocele → aspiration

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent periductal abscess → fistula; incomplete drainage → persistent infection
Proliferative lesions with atypia increase future cancer risk; simple cysts do not

rows.label: Prevention
items: Effective breast emptying during lactation; smoking cessation for recurrent periductal disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cancer: irregular fixed mass, retraction or suspicious nodes
Phyllodes: rapidly enlarging fibroepithelial mass requiring excision

table.title: Common benign findings
rows: Early postpartum; bilateral tense tender breasts, low fever

bone-tumors.name: Bone tumors
bone-tumors.scope: Osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, chondrosarcoma, giant cell tumor of bone, osteochondroma, osteoid osteoma, bone metastases, biopsy
bone-tumors.core: Persistent focal bone pain, a growing mass, or a destructive radiographic lesion requires planned evaluation before biopsy or fixation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Osteosarcoma: adolescence, hereditary retinoblastoma (RB1), prior radiation, Paget disease; chondrosarcoma: older adults
Hereditary multiple exostoses predispose to osteochondromas; most adult malignant bone lesions are metastases

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Night/rest pain**, enlarging mass, constitutional symptoms or pathologic fracture → concerning lesion
Osteoid osteoma: nocturnal pain relieved by NSAIDs; small cortical nidus
Osteochondroma: painless metaphyseal exostosis with medullary continuity; new growth after maturity concerning
Known cancer + constant back pain, vertebral point tenderness → **spinal metastasis**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Tumor lineage determines osteoid, cartilage or primitive-cell production; aggressive growth destroys cortex
Giant cell tumor: neoplastic stromal cells recruit osteoclast-like giant cells, causing locally aggressive osteolysis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Plain radiographs first**; assess location, margins, periosteal reaction and matrix
Aggressive lesion → MRI entire involved bone/adjacent joint; chest CT for lung metastases
★ **Orthopedic oncology plans biopsy tract**; core biopsy after imaging, before definitive treatment
CBC, ESR/CRP if infection suspected; normal labs do not exclude malignancy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Osteosarcoma → **neoadjuvant chemotherapy + wide resection**, then postoperative chemotherapy
Ewing → systemic chemotherapy plus surgery and/or radiation
Chondrosarcoma → wide surgical excision; conventional tumors relatively chemo/radioresistant
Symptomatic osteoid osteoma → radiofrequency ablation; asymptomatic osteochondroma → observation
Giant cell tumor → curettage/reconstruction; selected unresectable lesions → denosumab

rows.label: Complications
items: Pathologic fracture, neurovascular compromise, pulmonary metastases; limb surgery and chemotherapy morbidity
Mandible metastasis → mental nerve anesthesia (**numb chin**)

rows.label: Mimics
items: Osteomyelitis: infection markers, cultures; may closely resemble Ewing
Bone metastases: older adult, multiple lesions; myeloma: anemia, monoclonal protein
Unicameral bone cyst: child, lucent expansile proximal humerus lesion; pathologic fracture after minor trauma

bone-tumors.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

bowel-obstruction.name: Bowel obstruction
bowel-obstruction.scope: Small bowel obstruction (adhesions, hernia), large bowel obstruction (volvulus, malignancy), paralytic ileus, NG decompression, surgical management
bowel-obstruction.core: Colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, distention, and obstipation suggest mechanical obstruction; constant pain or systemic toxicity raises concern for strangulation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior abdominal surgery (**adhesions**, leading cause), incarcerated hernia, Crohn strictures → small-bowel obstruction
Colorectal malignancy, chronic constipation, institutionalization → large-bowel obstruction or sigmoid volvulus
Recent surgery, opioids, hypokalemia, severe systemic illness → ileus

rows.label: Clues
items: Early high-pitched sounds may become absent; proximal obstruction causes earlier vomiting, distal disease greater distention
★ **Peritonitis, fever, tachycardia, rising lactate**, or continuous severe pain → ischemia/perforation
Complete → **obstipation**, no flatus; partial may still pass stool/diarrhea, not excluding obstruction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Luminal blockage → upstream dilation, third spacing; closed loop compromises venous then arterial supply
Adynamic ileus reflects impaired motility without an anatomic transition point

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast** defines transition point, cause, and ischemic signs
CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, lactate; normal lactate cannot exclude early ischemia
Radiograph may show dilated loops/air-fluid levels, no rectal gas; CT more definitive if diagnosis uncertain
★ Massive colonic distention + **coffee-bean (inverted-U) loop** on radiograph → sigmoid volvulus
Pregnancy: plain radiograph acceptable first (minimal fetal dose); MRI if unclear; do not delay

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO, IV isotonic fluids, electrolyte correction**; NG decompression for significant vomiting/distention
★ Strangulation, perforation, closed loop, or incarcerated hernia → **urgent surgery** + ceftriaxone/metronidazole
Uncomplicated adhesive SBO → surgical observation, serial examination; water-soluble contrast helps predict resolution
Failure to improve during a short monitored trial, commonly up to 72 h → operation
Ileus → correct trigger, reduce opioids, mobilize; no operation solely for absent sounds

rows.label: Complications
items: Dehydration, AKI, hypokalemic alkalosis; bowel necrosis, perforation, sepsis
Recurrent adhesions; short-bowel syndrome after extensive resection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early postoperative ambulation, opioid-sparing analgesia, electrolyte correction; elective repair of symptomatic hernias

rows.label: Mimics
items: Gastroenteritis: prominent diarrhea, no focal transition point
Mesenteric ischemia: pain out of proportion before peritoneal signs
Ileus: hypoactive/absent sounds, gas throughout bowel including rectum
Diabetic autonomic neuropathy: dysmotility, dilated loops without transition point

table.title: Large-bowel branches
rows: Sigmoidoscopic detorsion, rectal tube → same-admission resection

breast-neoplasia.name: Breast neoplasia
breast-neoplasia.scope: Ductal carcinoma in situ, invasive ductal and lobular carcinoma, receptor status (ER, PR, HER2), metastatic disease (bone, visceral), surgical management, endocrine and chemotherapy
breast-neoplasia.core: A suspicious breast lesion requires core biopsy, assessment of invasion and ER/PR/HER2 status to guide local and systemic treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Increasing age, BRCA-related syndromes, close-relative family history (distant relative adds little), prior chest irradiation
**Combined estrogen-progestin therapy**, prolonged estrogen, postmenopausal obesity, alcohol; atypical proliferative lesions

rows.label: Clues
items: Painless hard irregular mass, skin/nipple retraction, unilateral bloody discharge or axillary node
★ Peau d’orange, diffuse erythema and edema → **inflammatory breast cancer**, even without discrete mass
Persistent unilateral eczematous nipple lesion → Paget disease; **full-thickness biopsy**, investigate underlying carcinoma

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Invasion through basement membrane enables lymphatic/hematogenous metastasis
ER/PR signaling and HER2 amplification create actionable tumor drivers; triple-negative tumors lack these targets

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Diagnostic mammography + targeted ultrasound** → core biopsy of suspicious lesion; pregnancy → **ultrasound first**
Pathology: invasion, grade, **ER/PR/HER2**; assess regional nodes clinically and with targeted imaging
Clinically node-negative invasive disease, including microinvasion ≤1 mm → sentinel node biopsy during definitive surgery
Distant staging scans for advanced disease or suspicious symptoms; not every small asymptomatic cancer
Axillary node adenocarcinoma, normal mammogram → occult breast primary; breast MRI

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Early: lumpectomy + radiation or mastectomy; **positive margins → reexcision** before adjuvant therapy
ER-positive → tamoxifen or postmenopausal aromatase inhibitor; chemotherapy based on stage/biology
★ HER2-positive → **trastuzumab-based** treatment, monitor LVEF; triple-negative → chemotherapy ± pembrolizumab if higher-risk
Locally advanced → neoadjuvant treatment, then surgery/radiation; large residual + palpable nodes → **mastectomy + axillary dissection**
Bone metastases → **zoledronate/denosumab**; systemic treatment by receptors, chemotherapy for visceral crisis

rows.label: Complications
items: Metastases to bone (often **mixed lytic–blastic**), lung, liver, brain; surgery/radiation → lymphedema
Tamoxifen → VTE/endometrial cancer; aromatase inhibitors → bone loss; trastuzumab → cardiomyopathy
Prior cancer + severe hypercalcemia, lytic lesions → recurrence; thiazide/calcium supplements cause only mild elevation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Age/risk-based screening, genetic counseling for suggestive pedigree; selected high-risk patients → chemoprevention
BRCA-related very high risk → discuss risk-reducing surgery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Mastitis: lactation-associated tenderness/fever, improves with antibiotics
Fat necrosis: trauma/surgery history; biopsy if discordant imaging

table.title: Histologic distinctions
rows: Bilateral risk marker; discohesive lobular cells
Surveillance/risk reduction if concordant; later cancer usually ductal

colorectal-cancer-screening.name: Colorectal cancer screening
colorectal-cancer-screening.scope: Average-risk screening age 45-75, colonoscopy, FIT, high-risk screening (family history, Lynch syndrome, IBD), post-polypectomy surveillance
colorectal-cancer-screening.core: Screen average-risk adults ages 45–75; every positive noncolonoscopy screening test requires diagnostic colonoscopy.

rows.label: Who
items: Average risk: no CRC/adenoma history, IBD or hereditary syndrome; FDR = first-degree relative
★ Symptoms or iron deficiency anemia → **diagnostic evaluation**, regardless of screening age
FDR CRC/advanced polyp <60 or ≥2 affected FDRs → high-risk family pathway

rows.label: Start/stop
items: Ages 76–85: individualize by health, preference and prior screening; stop after 85
★ High-risk family → start **40 or 10 years before youngest diagnosis**, whichever earlier
Family-risk colonoscopy every 5 years; one FDR ≥60 → start 40, routine intervals

rows.label: Test
items: ★ **Colonoscopy every 10 years** or **FIT annually** are common strategies
Stool DNA–FIT every 1–3 years; CT colonography every 5 years
Flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 years, or every 10 years plus annual FIT

rows.label: IF positive
items: Positive FIT/stool DNA/CT study → colonoscopy; repeating stool test cannot clear the result
Post-polypectomy intervals assume complete removal, adequate preparation and high-quality examination

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Lynch: colonoscopy roughly age 20–25 every 1–2 years; gene/family history can modify
Colonic IBD: surveillance about 8 years after onset; PSC → begin at diagnosis
Routine stool testing between scheduled high-quality surveillance colonoscopies adds little benefit

colorectal-polyps-and-polyposis-syndrome.name: Colorectal polyps and polyposis syndromes
colorectal-polyps-and-polyposis-syndrome.scope: Adenomatous polyps, serrated polyps, familial adenomatous polyposis, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, juvenile polyposis
colorectal-polyps-and-polyposis-syndrome.core: Colorectal polyps differ in malignant potential; numerous lesions or characteristic extraintestinal findings suggest an inherited cancer syndrome.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, family history, obesity, smoking; pathogenic germline variants in hereditary polyposis

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually incidental; occult bleeding or iron-deficiency anemia; large distal polyps may prolapse
Childhood painless rectal bleeding → solitary juvenile polyp; recurrent pain → hamartoma-associated intussusception
★ **Mucocutaneous lip pigmentation** with hamartomatous polyps → Peutz-Jeghers
Serrated crypts: proximal sessile lesions premalignant, unlike typical small distal hyperplastic polyps

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Conventional adenomas progress through dysplasia; sessile serrated lesions follow a distinct molecular pathway
Hamartomas contain disorganized native tissue; syndromic forms carry cancer risk despite benign-appearing histology

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Colonoscopy with complete polypectomy and histology** defines type and surveillance
Advanced adenoma: ≥10 mm, villous component, or high-grade dysplasia
Numerous adenomas, young age, syndromic features → genetic counseling/testing
≥5 juvenile colorectal polyps, other GI juvenile polyps, or family history → juvenile polyposis evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Remove adenomatous/serrated lesions; incomplete or unresectable lesion → advanced endoscopy or surgery
FAP → **prophylactic colectomy** when burden/dysplasia cannot be controlled; continue retained-rectum surveillance
Hamartomatous syndromes → endoscopic removal of large/symptomatic polyps; surgery for obstruction or uncontrolled burden

rows.label: Complications
items: Colorectal cancer; postpolypectomy bleeding/perforation; intussusception and anemia in hamartomatous disease
FAP → duodenal cancer, desmoid tumors; Peutz-Jeghers → pancreatic, breast and gynecologic cancers

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Family cascade testing; syndrome-specific colon and upper-GI surveillance
Low-risk 1–2 small tubular adenomas → repeat colonoscopy 7–10 years after high-quality examination
Advanced adenoma → generally 3 years; shorten for large piecemeal resection or numerous lesions

rows.label: Mimics
items: Sporadic hyperplastic polyp: small rectosigmoid lesion, usually negligible cancer risk
Lynch syndrome: few polyps, mismatch-repair defect, colorectal/endometrial cancers

colorectal-polyps-and-polyposis-syndrome.evidence: Surveillance checked 2026-10-30: [US Multi-Society Task Force, 2020](https://www.asge.org/home/resources/publications/guidelines/recommendations-for-follow-up-after-colonoscopy-and-polypectomy-a-consensus-update-by-the-us-multi-society-task-force-on-colorectal-cancer); syndromes: established teaching.

dyspepsia-and-peptic-ulcer-disease.name: Dyspepsia and peptic ulcer disease
dyspepsia-and-peptic-ulcer-disease.scope: Uninvestigated dyspepsia (age < 60 test-and-treat vs age >= 60 endoscopy), Helicobacter pylori testing and eradication, gastric and duodenal ulcers
dyspepsia-and-peptic-ulcer-disease.core: Epigastric discomfort may reflect functional dyspepsia or acid-peptic ulceration; age and bleeding risk determine noninvasive testing versus endoscopy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: H pylori, NSAIDs/aspirin; smoking impairs healing
Prior ulcer bleeding, anticoagulants, older age amplify NSAID harm; severe physiologic stress causes ICU ulcers

rows.label: Clues
items: Epigastric burning, early satiety, nausea; meal timing cannot reliably distinguish ulcer location
★ **Alarm**: hematemesis/melena, positive occult blood, dysphagia, persistent vomiting, weight loss, iron-deficiency anemia
Sudden rigid abdomen → perforation
Early satiety, nonbilious vomiting, succussion splash, gastric distention → gastric outlet obstruction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: H pylori or prostaglandin depletion weakens mucosal defenses against acid-pepsin injury
Antral-predominant infection increases acid; corpus-predominant inflammation may cause atrophy

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ New dyspepsia **≥60 years or any alarm feature → upper endoscopy**
★ Under 60 without concerning features → **urea breath or stool antigen test**
Hold PPI 2 weeks and antibiotics/bismuth 4 weeks before active-infection testing; serology cannot confirm eradication
Gastric ulcer → biopsy to exclude malignancy; duodenal ulcers rarely malignant
Refractory/recurrent multiple ulcers + diarrhea → fasting gastrin with careful PPI interpretation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ H pylori → **14-day bismuth quadruple**: PPI + bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole
Avoid empiric clarithromycin/levofloxacin regimens unless susceptibility demonstrated
Negative infection test or persistent symptoms after eradication → PPI trial; functional symptoms may need TCA
Stop NSAID; ulcer healing → PPI; active bleeding → resuscitation, IV PPI, urgent endoscopic hemostasis
Perforation → IV fluids, ceftriaxone/metronidazole, urgent surgery; no elective diagnostic endoscopy

rows.label: Complications
items: Hemorrhage, perforation, penetration, outlet obstruction from scarring/fibrosis; H pylori → gastric cancer, MALT lymphoma

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Confirm eradication ≥4 weeks after antibiotics** with breath/stool test, off PPI as above
Necessary NSAID + high GI risk → concurrent PPI; use lowest effective NSAID exposure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Biliary colic: episodic RUQ pain, gallstones on ultrasound
ACS: exertional epigastric pressure, ischemic ECG/troponin findings

dyspepsia-and-peptic-ulcer-disease.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACG H pylori update (2024)](https://gi.org/journals-publications/ebgi/schoenfeld_sep2024/); dyspepsia age threshold established ACG/CAG teaching.

esophageal-motility-disorders.name: Esophageal motility disorders
esophageal-motility-disorders.scope: Achalasia, diffuse esophageal spasm, hypercontractile esophagus, Zenker diverticulum, manometry, barium swallow
esophageal-motility-disorders.core: Dysphagia to solids and liquids from onset suggests impaired motility; progressive solids-first dysphagia suggests mechanical obstruction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Achalasia often idiopathic; Chagas disease can destroy enteric ganglia
Older age predisposes to Zenker diverticulum; opioids can produce spastic motility patterns

rows.label: Clues
items: Achalasia: regurgitated undigested food, nocturnal cough, weight loss
★ Zenker: **halitosis, cervical gurgling, aspiration**, retained food hours after eating
Spastic disorders: intermittent dysphagia and squeezing chest pain; hot/cold liquids may provoke

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Achalasia: loss of inhibitory myenteric neurons → impaired LES relaxation and absent peristalsis
Zenker: cricopharyngeal dysfunction → mucosal herniation through Killian triangle

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Esophageal symptoms → **upper endoscopy** to exclude stricture/cancer before motility testing
★ **High-resolution manometry** confirms functional disorder after structural disease excluded
Barium swallow defines emptying; suspected Zenker → **barium study before endoscopy**
Rapid weight loss, older onset or difficult LES passage → evaluate pseudoachalasia with CT/endoscopic ultrasound
Chest pain → exclude ACS before labeling esophageal spasm

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Achalasia → pneumatic dilation, Heller myotomy + fundoplication, or **POEM**
Botulinum toxin for achalasia when procedural risk precludes durable treatment
Spastic disorders → remove opioid trigger, treat reflux; diltiazem or nitrates for persistent symptoms
Symptomatic Zenker → **cricopharyngeal myotomy + diverticulectomy** or endoscopic septotomy; no dilation or blind NG tube

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition; longstanding achalasia → increased squamous cancer risk
Dilation/myotomy → perforation; myotomy, especially POEM → gastroesophageal reflux

rows.label: Prevention
items: Eat slowly, chew thoroughly, remain upright after meals to reduce regurgitation/aspiration

rows.label: Mimics
items: Esophageal cancer: progressive solids-first symptoms; obstructing lesion
Scleroderma: hypotensive LES with reflux, distal aperistalsis

table.title: Manometry and contrast findings
rows: Impaired LES relaxation; absent normal peristalsis

esophageal-motility-disorders.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACG achalasia guideline](https://gi.org/guideline/diagnosis-and-management-of-achalasia/); other disorders established teaching.

esophageal-perforation.name: Esophageal perforation
esophageal-perforation.scope: Boerhaave syndrome, iatrogenic perforation, mediastinitis, gastrografin esophagography, emergent surgical repair
esophageal-perforation.core: Severe chest pain after vomiting or esophageal instrumentation, with systemic toxicity or mediastinal air, is an esophageal emergency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Endoscopy, dilation, foreign bodies, caustic injury; forceful emesis causes spontaneous Boerhaave rupture
Underlying stricture or malignancy increases instrumentation-related injury risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Tachycardia, fever, dyspnea, odynophagia; neck swelling or palpable crepitus
★ **Left pleural effusion**, pneumomediastinum or subcutaneous emphysema after retching
Hypotension, rising lactate, organ dysfunction → uncontrolled contamination and sepsis
Classic vomiting–pain–emphysema triad often incomplete; absence does not exclude rupture

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Full-thickness tear releases saliva, gastric contents and bacteria into mediastinum/pleura
Boerhaave typically affects distal posterolateral esophagus; contamination causes chemical then infectious mediastinitis

rows.label: Dx
items: **Upright chest x-ray first** for mediastinal/pleural air; normal early film does not exclude → contrast study
★ Stable suspected leak → **CT chest with water-soluble oral contrast** or water-soluble esophagram
Gastrografin study negative with persistent suspicion → thin barium study to detect small leaks
Avoid routine diagnostic endoscopy when insufflation could enlarge an uncontained tear

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO**, IV fluids, IV piperacillin–tazobactam, urgent thoracic/general surgery consultation
★ Free pleural/mediastinal leak (even stable) or shock → **operative repair + drainage**; chest tube inadequate
Contained leak without sepsis → antibiotics, drainage ± endoscopic closure/stent; older questions may expect surgery
IV proton-pump inhibitor; enteral feeding distal to leak or parenteral nutrition
Avoid blind nasogastric placement; decompression, if needed, under specialist guidance

rows.label: Complications
items: Mediastinitis, empyema, septic shock, multiorgan failure; delay markedly worsens outcomes
Persistent fistula, esophageal stricture and malnutrition after healing

rows.label: Prevention
items: Careful procedural technique; prompt evaluation of new pain following esophageal instrumentation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Mallory–Weiss: mucosal tear causing hematemesis without mediastinal contamination
ACS: ischemic ECG/troponin pattern; no contrast leak
Acute aortic syndrome: vascular abnormality on CT angiography

esophageal-perforation.evidence: Not checked online; established emergency esophageal management.

gallstone-disease.name: Gallstone disease
gallstone-disease.scope: Biliary colic, acute cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, cholangitis, gallstone pancreatitis
gallstone-disease.core: Gallstone location determines the syndrome: transient cystic obstruction, gallbladder inflammation, common-duct obstruction/infection, or pancreatic inflammation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, female sex, pregnancy, obesity, rapid weight loss, ileal disease/resection
Hemolysis/cirrhosis → pigment stones; critical illness/TPN → acalculous cholecystitis

rows.label: Clues
items: Postprandial RUQ/epigastric discomfort radiating to back or right shoulder; assess fever and jaundice
★ **Fever + RUQ pain + jaundice** → cholangitis; hypotension/confusion → severe infection
Pancreatitis: persistent epigastric pain radiating to back, vomiting; ALT >150 supports biliary cause

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Cholesterol supersaturation or pigment precipitation creates calculi; obstruction location dictates organ injury
Infected obstructed bile ducts require drainage because antibiotics cannot reliably sterilize a closed system

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **RUQ ultrasound first**; CBC, bilirubin/alkaline phosphatase, AST/ALT, lipase
Suspected cholecystitis with equivocal ultrasound → HIDA; nonvisualized gallbladder supports cystic-duct obstruction
Intermediate common-duct stone probability → MRCP or EUS; ERCP reserved primarily for treatment
★ Direct intervention: **stone seen, cholangitis, or bilirubin >4 mg/dL plus dilated duct**
Post-cholecystectomy jaundice + dilated ducts → retained stone/duct injury → **ERCP**; HIDA only for bile leak

rows.label: Tx
items: Analgesia, fluids, antiemetics; infection → ceftriaxone/metronidazole or piperacillin/tazobactam
★ **Cholangitis → urgent biliary drainage**, immediately after stabilization if shock; do not await antibiotic response
Poor surgical candidate with acute cholecystitis → percutaneous cholecystostomy
★ Gallstone pancreatitis → supportive care, early oral feeding; **no urgent ERCP without cholangitis/persistent obstruction**

rows.label: Complications
items: Empyema, gangrene, perforation, abscess, septic shock; pancreatitis → necrosis/organ failure
Cholecystoenteric fistula → gallstone ileus; imaging: bowel obstruction, pneumobilia, ectopic stone
ERCP → pancreatitis/bleeding/perforation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintain healthy weight; avoid rapid weight loss; selected bariatric patients → ursodiol prophylaxis
After duct clearance → cholecystectomy; after mild biliary pancreatitis → same-admission cholecystectomy
Asymptomatic uncomplicated stones → observation; no routine prophylactic surgery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hepatitis: marked aminotransferase elevation, no obstructing stone
PUD: burning epigastric pain, ulcer on endoscopy
Inferior MI: ischemic ECG/troponin changes, cardiovascular risk

table.title: Localizing obstruction
rows: Persistent >6 hours, Murphy sign, wall thickening
Cholestatic labs, duct stone/dilation; no infection
ERCP extraction or operative duct clearance
Inflamed gallbladder without stones; critically ill

gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.scope: Clinical diagnosis, empiric PPI trial, lifestyle measures, alarm symptoms, Barrett esophagus screening, 24-hour pH monitoring
gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.core: Heartburn and acid regurgitation after meals or recumbency suggest reflux; complications or diagnostic uncertainty change the testing pathway.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Obesity, pregnancy, hiatal hernia, smoking; drugs reducing lower esophageal sphincter tone
Late large meals and individual food triggers exacerbate symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: Sour taste, nocturnal symptoms, chest discomfort; chronic nocturnal/supine cough may be sole symptom
★ **Dysphagia, odynophagia, bleeding, weight loss**, persistent vomiting, anemia → endoscopy
Exertional chest pain → cardiac evaluation; nocturnal burning relieved upright → empiric acid suppression
Infant spit-up + **poor weight gain** → pathologic GERD; pyloric stenosis: projectile vomiting at 3–6 weeks

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Transient lower sphincter relaxation and impaired barrier allow gastric contents into esophagus
Acid exposure → erosions; chronic injury may produce intestinal metaplasia

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical symptoms without alarms → **8-week empiric once-daily PPI trial**
Alarm features or failed treatment → upper endoscopy; biopsies evaluate alternative mucosal disease
★ Unproven GERD + normal endoscopy → **ambulatory pH monitoring off PPI**
Proven GERD with refractory symptoms → impedance-pH testing on PPI after optimizing use
Manometry evaluates motility and precedes antireflux surgery; not the primary reflux diagnostic test

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Omeprazole 30–60 minutes before breakfast**; verify adherence before escalation
Intermittent mild symptoms → antacid or famotidine; persistent breakthrough → optimize/split PPI schedule
Weight reduction if overweight; avoid meals within 2–3 hours of bedtime, elevate bed head
Objective reflux with regurgitation or **recurrent aspiration** despite drugs → fundoplication; gastrostomy alone inadequate
Severe erosive esophagitis → long-term PPI or surgery; step down uncomplicated controlled disease

rows.label: Complications
items: Erosive esophagitis, peptic stricture, Barrett esophagus, adenocarcinoma
Stricture → **endoscopy + biopsy to exclude cancer**, then dilation plus acid suppression
Barrett dysplasia → endoscopic eradication; low-grade, older questions: EGD/biopsy at 6 months, even after fundoplication

rows.label: Prevention
items: Barrett screening: chronic reflux + ≥3 additional risks: male, >50, White, tobacco, obesity, first-degree family history
Smoking cessation and symptom-directed trigger reduction; routine endoscopy unnecessary for every reflux patient

rows.label: Mimics
items: Achalasia: solids and liquids dysphagia, impaired sphincter relaxation
Eosinophilic esophagitis: atopy, food impaction, eosinophilic biopsy
Functional heartburn: normal reflux burden and no symptom association

gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.evidence: Not checked online; established ACG reflux and Barrett screening teaching.

gastrointestinal-bleeding.name: Gastrointestinal bleeding
gastrointestinal-bleeding.scope: Upper GI bleeding (PUD, varices, Mallory-Weiss), lower GI bleeding (diverticular, angiodysplasia, hemorrhoids), fluid and transfusion thresholds, endoscopy
gastrointestinal-bleeding.core: Hematemesis, melena, or hematochezia → assess hemodynamics before localizing; brisk upper bleeding can present as bright red rectal blood.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: NSAIDs/H pylori → ulcers; cirrhosis → varices; forceful retching → mucosal tear
Anticoagulants/antiplatelets increase severity; older age favors diverticula or angiodysplasia

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Syncope, orthostasis, shock** signal major loss; initial hemoglobin may remain normal
Epigastric pain supports ulcer; painless bleeding favors vascular sources
Recurrent occult loss → iron deficiency
**Melena**, elevated BUN/creatinine ratio → upper source; bilious NG aspirate argues against upper bleeding

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Mucosal injury, portal-pressure collaterals, or fragile vessels rupture into GI lumen
Volume depletion → reduced perfusion; ongoing bleeding may require massive transfusion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Two large-bore IVs, CBC, type/cross, coagulation tests**, serial hemoglobin; resuscitate before procedures
Upper source → EGD within 24 hours after stabilization; suspected varices → within 12 hours
★ Ongoing hemodynamically significant hematochezia → **CT angiography → embolization** if active extravasation
Stable lower bleeding → bowel preparation and nonemergent colonoscopy; routine <24-hour colonoscopy adds no benefit
Rectal bleeding mixed with stool, age ≥45 → colonoscopy; negative FOBT does not exclude neoplasia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Crystalloid initially; stable nonischemic adults → **RBC transfusion at hemoglobin <7 g/dL**
Exsanguination or post-crystalloid shock → **RBCs** regardless of hemoglobin, not vasopressors; cardiac ischemia → higher threshold
Severe anticoagulant bleeding → drug-specific reversal; uncontrolled varices → balloon tamponade as temporary bridge only
Failed endoscopy → IR/surgery; massive unlocalized lower bleeding → **total abdominal colectomy**, not segmental
Suspected ulcer → IV PPI; endoscopic hemostasis for active bleeding/visible vessel, then high-dose PPI

rows.label: Complications
items: Rebleeding, aspiration, myocardial ischemia, AKI; variceal bleeding → infection
Massive transfusion → hypocalcemia, hypothermia, coagulopathy; embolization → bowel ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Eradicate H pylori and confirm cure; avoid NSAIDs; PPI for high-risk users
After variceal control: nonselective beta-blocker plus repeat banding; recurrent bleeding → TIPS

rows.label: Mimics
items: Iron/bismuth: dark stool without blood loss
Hemoptysis: coughing frothy blood rather than vomiting
Swallowed epistaxis: nasal source on examination

table.title: Source-specific branches
rows: Postretching tear; Boerhaave instead: chest pain, crepitus
Liver trauma + jaundice; blood from ampulla

gastrointestinal-bleeding.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACG lower GI bleeding 2023](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36735555/), [ACS transfusion guidance 2025](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009).

genitourinary-trauma.name: Genitourinary trauma
genitourinary-trauma.scope: Posterior urethral injury, anterior urethral injury, bladder rupture, retrograde urethrography, renal trauma, testicular trauma
genitourinary-trauma.core: Hematuria or inability to void after trauma requires localization of urinary injury before instrumentation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pelvic fracture → posterior urethra/bladder; straddle injury → anterior bulbar urethra
Deceleration, flank impact or penetrating wounds → renal/collecting-system injury
Blunt scrotal trauma → testicular rupture; empty bladder better protected than distended bladder
Hysterectomy/pelvic surgery → ureteral ligation: flank pain, fever, unilateral hydroureteronephrosis; not pyelonephritis

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Blood at urethral meatus**, retention, perineal/scrotal hematoma or high-riding prostate → urethral injury
Gross hematuria with pelvic fracture → suspect bladder rupture
Flank ecchymosis, tenderness or lower rib fractures suggest renal injury
Scrotal swelling, bruising and loss of normal contour suggest testicular rupture

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Pelvic shearing disrupts membranous urethra; direct compression splits the bulbar segment
Intraperitoneal urine leakage irritates peritoneum; blood loss can cause shock despite modest hematuria

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected urethral injury → **retrograde urethrogram before Foley**; no blind repeated attempts
★ Stable gross hematuria + pelvic fracture → **retrograde CT/plain cystography**
Blunt flank trauma → **urinalysis**; stable, no hematuria → **no further testing** unless high-energy deceleration
Stable gross hematuria, or microscopic + hypotension → contrast CT abdomen/pelvis with delayed images, not laparotomy
Testicular injury → Doppler ultrasound; absent flow or high clinical suspicion → immediate exploration

rows.label: Tx
items: Hemodynamic instability → trauma resuscitation and urgent operative/angiographic hemorrhage control
Urethral disruption → urology, suprapubic drainage or selected endoscopic realignment
★ **Intraperitoneal bladder rupture → surgical repair**; uncomplicated extraperitoneal rupture → catheter drainage
Stable renal injuries → observation; ongoing arterial bleeding → selective embolization
Testicular rupture → urgent exploration, repair and removal of nonviable tissue

rows.label: Complications
items: Urethral stricture, erectile dysfunction, incontinence; urinary extravasation → infection or urinoma
Delayed renal bleeding, hypertension or kidney loss; testicular atrophy and infertility

rows.label: Prevention
items: Protective equipment; safe catheter technique; follow-up for stricture after urethral injury

rows.label: Mimics
items: Testicular torsion: absent flow with spermatic-cord twist; also surgical emergency
Nontraumatic stone: colicky flank pain without injury mechanism

hyperbilirubinemia.name: Hyperbilirubinemia
hyperbilirubinemia.scope: Gilbert syndrome, Crigler-Najjar, Dubin-Johnson, Rotor, unconjugated vs conjugated, biliary atresia
hyperbilirubinemia.core: Fractionate bilirubin first: indirect elevation reflects production or conjugation problems; direct elevation requires assessment of hepatobiliary excretion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Fasting, illness or dehydration triggers Gilbert jaundice; family history suggests inherited bilirubin disorders
Persistent infant jaundice can reflect biliary atresia even after initially reassuring appearance

rows.label: Clues
items: Indirect bilirubin is albumin-bound and absent from urine; direct bilirubin can darken urine
★ Infant **pale/acholic stools**, dark urine, hepatomegaly → obstructive cholestasis
Pruritus, pale stools and elevated alkaline phosphatase suggest impaired bile flow
Severe neonatal indirect elevation with lethargy, poor feeding or abnormal tone → bilirubin neurotoxicity

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Heme breakdown yields unconjugated pigment; hepatic UGT conjugation enables biliary elimination
Unbound unconjugated bilirubin crosses the immature blood–brain barrier; conjugated bilirubin does not cause kernicterus
Large hematoma/cephalhematoma resorption → bilirubin overproduction, indirect jaundice

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Total/direct bilirubin**, AST/ALT, alkaline phosphatase/GGT; CBC/reticulocytes/LDH for suspected hemolysis
Isolated mild indirect elevation with normal liver tests and no hemolysis → Gilbert diagnosis
★ Jaundice beyond 2 weeks → fractionate; **direct ≥1 mg/dL at 2–4 weeks** → urgent referral
Infant cholestasis → ultrasound; biliary atresia assessment may require biopsy and operative cholangiography
Adult conjugated elevation with pain/obstruction → RUQ ultrasound before advanced duct imaging

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected biliary atresia → urgent pediatric hepatology/surgery; **early Kasai portoenterostomy**
Severe neonatal indirect, even Coombs-positive → **phototherapy** first; exchange: failure, critical level, encephalopathy
Crigler–Najjar I → intensive phototherapy, definitive liver transplant; type II responds to phenobarbital
Gilbert, Dubin–Johnson and Rotor → reassurance once competing pathology excluded
Cholestasis → nutritional support, fat-soluble vitamins and cause-specific treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Indirect neonatal hyperbilirubinemia → acute encephalopathy/kernicterus
Untreated atresia → cirrhosis, portal hypertension, liver failure

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Inspect stool color and fractionate persistent infant jaundice; never label conjugated jaundice physiologic

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hemolysis: anemia, reticulocytosis, low haptoglobin; newborn ABO: mother O, baby A/B, Coombs-positive
Choledochal cyst: cystic/dilated extrahepatic ducts on ultrasound
Physiologic jaundice: indirect, after 24 h, peaks days 3–5, thriving; transient UGT immaturity
Breast-milk jaundice: indirect, thriving; direct elevation excludes it

hyperbilirubinemia.evidence: Infant referral checked 2026-10-30: [AAP 2025](https://publications.aap.org/aapnews/news/pdfDownload/31302); inherited syndromes established teaching.

hyperthyroidism.name: Hyperthyroidism and thyrotoxicosis
hyperthyroidism.scope: Graves disease, toxic multinodular goiter, toxic adenoma, subacute thyroiditis, thyroid storm, beta-blockers, thionamides, radioactive iodine
hyperthyroidism.core: Excess circulating thyroid hormone → heat intolerance, weight loss despite appetite, tremor, and tachycardia; hormone overproduction differs from destructive release.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autoimmune history, female sex; older age favors autonomous nodules
Iodine load, amiodarone, exogenous thyroid hormone; infection/surgery can precipitate storm

rows.label: Clues
items: Hyperreflexia, lid lag, onycholysis, frequent stools, proximal weakness, widened pulse pressure; older adults: apathetic
★ **Thyroid storm**: fever, delirium, severe tachyarrhythmia, vomiting, heart failure; clinical diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Increased tissue metabolic activity and beta-adrenergic sensitivity explain systemic manifestations
Thionamides block thyroid peroxidase; PTU also reduces peripheral T4 → T3 conversion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TSH first → free T4**, total T3 if T4 normal; suppressed TSH with elevated hormones
TRAb establishes Graves; uncertain cause → **Doppler ultrasound** or radioiodine uptake (not if pregnant/lactating)
Low uptake: thyroiditis/exogenous hormone; low thyroglobulin supports exogenous ingestion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptom control: **propranolol**; caution in asthma or decompensated HF
★ Storm → ICU, cooling/fluids, beta-blockade if tolerated, **PTU → iodine ≥1 hour later**, hydrocortisone
Radioiodine contraindicated during pregnancy/lactation; significant active orbitopathy favors another definitive treatment
Compression/suspicious nodule → thyroidectomy after control; pregnancy: first-trimester PTU, later methimazole

rows.label: Complications
items: AF, embolism, osteoporosis, mild hypercalcemia, cardiomyopathy; radioiodine often → hypothyroidism
★ Thionamides: **fever/sore throat → stop drug, urgent CBC**; PTU → severe hepatotoxicity
Pregnancy: thionamides/TRAb cross placenta → **fetal goiter**, impaired swallowing, polyhydramnios

rows.label: Prevention
items: Monitor free T4 early during treatment; TSH recovery lags
Smoking cessation for orbitopathy; definitive treatment before planned pregnancy when feasible

rows.label: Mimics
items: Panic disorder: episodic symptoms without thyroid biochemical abnormalities
Pheochromocytoma: paroxysmal headache, sweating, severe hypertension
Menopause: hot flashes with menstrual transition, normal thyroid testing
Orbital pseudotumor: involves muscle bellies and tendons; Graves spares tendons

table.title: Etiology determines treatment
rows: Diffuse uptake; bruit, orbitopathy, pretibial myxedema, acropachy (clubbing)
One hot nodule, suppressed surrounding tissue
NSAID; prednisone if severe; no thionamides

hypocalcemia.name: Hypocalcemia
hypocalcemia.scope: Hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, post-thyroidectomy, hypomagnesemia
hypocalcemia.core: Low ionized calcium causes neuromuscular irritability and QT prolongation; severe symptoms require IV calcium while the cause is corrected.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Thyroid/parathyroid surgery, autoimmune hypoparathyroidism, DiGeorge syndrome
Vitamin D deficiency from low intake, malabsorption, limited sun; CKD, pancreatitis, massive citrate transfusion
Severe hypomagnesemia from alcoholism, diarrhea, PPIs, diuretics; bisphosphonates/denosumab can precipitate deficiency

rows.label: Clues
items: Perioral tingling, distal paresthesias, muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm
★ **Trousseau sign**: cuff-induced carpal spasm; Chvostek sign is less specific
★ Severe: **seizures, laryngospasm, arrhythmias**; ECG shows prolonged QT
Post-thyroidectomy tingling or stridor requires immediate calcium assessment rather than simple reassurance

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced extracellular calcium lowers nerve excitation threshold; myocardial repolarization is prolonged
Low magnesium impairs both PTH secretion and action, making calcium replacement alone ineffective

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Ionized calcium**, Mg, phosphate, creatinine, PTH, 25-hydroxyvitamin D
Low albumin lowers total calcium, not necessarily ionized; correction formulas unreliable in critical illness
Alkalosis increases albumin binding → symptomatic low ionized calcium despite unchanged total concentration
Interpret PTH relative to calcium: normal PTH can be inappropriately low during hypocalcemia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic, severe, or ECG changes → **IV calcium gluconate with ECG monitoring**
Mild stable disease → oral calcium; nutritional vitamin D deficiency → cholecalciferol/ergocalciferol
Hypoparathyroidism or advanced CKD → **calcitriol** plus calcium; coordinate phosphate management
★ **Replace magnesium** when deficient; correct underlying cause, avoid overcorrection

rows.label: Complications
items: Tetany, seizures, ventricular arrhythmias; chronic deficiency can cause cataracts and basal ganglia calcification
Overreplacement → hypercalciuria, nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis; monitor serum and urine calcium

rows.label: Prevention
items: Monitor calcium after neck surgery and antiresorptive treatment; ensure sufficient vitamin D/calcium intake
Chronic hypoparathyroidism: target symptom control with low-normal serum calcium, avoiding renal calcium loading

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hyperventilation syndrome: transient alkalosis-related ionized reduction; assess precipitating illness
Seizure disorder: no biochemical calcium explanation; pseudohypocalcemia: normal ionized level

hypocalcemia.evidence: Not checked online; established endocrine teaching.

hyponatremia.name: Hyponatremia
hyponatremia.scope: Hypovolemic, euvolemic (SIADH, primary polydipsia), hypervolemic, acute vs chronic, hypertonic saline indications
hyponatremia.core: Low serum sodium reflects excess water relative to sodium; symptoms and duration determine urgency before the cause determines maintenance treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Thiazides, SSRIs, carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine, oxytocin; **hypotonic IV D5W**, postoperative state, exercise + excess water
Pulmonary/CNS disease; **small cell lung cancer** (ectopic ADH); heart failure, cirrhosis, renal failure

rows.label: Clues
items: Nausea, headache, gait instability; seizures, coma or marked confusion indicate severe cerebral edema
Orthostasis/dry mucosa suggest depletion; edema/ascites suggest excess extracellular fluid
SIADH: clinically euvolemic with inappropriately concentrated urine despite hypo-osmolality
Massive water intake, often psychiatric illness; urine osmolality below serum still favors polydipsia, even if >100

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hypotonic extracellular fluid drives water into brain; chronic adaptation makes rapid correction dangerous
ADH-mediated water retention or intake exceeding renal dilution capacity lowers sodium concentration
Low effective volume (heart failure, cirrhosis, diarrhea) → baroreceptor ADH release; total-body sodium high in edema

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Serum osmolality first: **<275 mOsm/kg** confirms hypotonicity; assess glucose and volume status
Hyperglycemia → translocational hyponatremia; severe hyperlipidemia/proteinemia → pseudohyponatremia
★ Urine osmolality **<100** → polydipsia/low solute; ≥100 → persistent ADH activity
Urine Na <20–30 suggests low effective arterial volume; >30 suggests renal loss or SIADH
Exclude adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism and renal failure before diagnosing SIADH; diuretics confound urine Na

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe neurologic symptoms → **3% saline bolus**, repeated for initial Na rise 4–6 mEq/L
